courses.repertoire: As White: the Giuoco Pianissimo, with c3, d3 and a slow build-up. As Black: 3...Bc5, then ...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7.
courses.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4: the bishop aims at f7, the weakest square near Black's king.

why.text:
As White, the Italian follows the opening principles: develop quickly, castle early, and aim the bishop at f7, the square only Black's king defends. The slow Giuoco Pianissimo taught here avoids the long forcing lines of the open game, so one plan works against almost everything. The opening goes back to Greco in the 1620s, and top players have favored it since the Berlin Defense blunted the Ruy Lopez in Kramnik's 2000 world title match.

As Black, 3...Bc5 is the most natural reply: the bishop takes its best diagonal and aims at f2, just as White's aims at f7. It avoids the sharp 4.Ng5 lines of the Two Knights Defense, and in most games you can copy White's quiet setup. Only the Center attack and the Evans Gambit need exact moves.

rows: 4.c3 and 5.d3, castle, Re1. Drop the bishop to b3 before ...Na5 or ...b5 can trade it.
4.d3, not 4.Ng5. 4...Bc5 5.c3 is the main line. Against ...Na5, Bb5, Ba4 and Bc2 keep the bishop.
4...Nf6, then ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. Against 5.d4, take with the bishop: 5...Bxd4.
5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+, then ...d5. Against 7.Nc3, take the e4 pawn.
4...Nf6 and ...d6. Against 5.Bg5, ...h6 and, if needed, ...g5 before you castle.
4...Bxb4 5.c3 Ba5, then give the pawn back with ...d5.
4...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. The fork trick 5.Nxe5? fails to 6...Nxc4!

why.text:
As Black, you get a solid position with no weak pawns, so trades suit you. Unlike in the French, your light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6.

As White, you meet the Caro-Kann in about 9% of your 1.e4 games. You can choose the kind of game you want, from a space advantage to sharp sidelines full of traps.

rows: White develops quietly: Nf3, Be2 and castling before anything sharp. Black answers ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6, then brings a knight to f5.

Black plays ...c5 before developing the bishop. After c3 and ...cxd4, ...Bg4 pins the knight that guards d4.
White plays c4 and, after the trades on d5, keeps an isolated d-pawn. Black develops with ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and ...Bg4.
4...Bf5 develops the bishop at once and lets White chase it with Ng3. Club players then often play Nf3, Bd3 and a bishop trade instead of the sharp h4.
Black accepts doubled f-pawns for quick development: ...Bd6, castling and ...Bg4.
White develops before playing d4. With the queen on e2 and a bishop on c4, White sets traps on e7 and f7.
After 4.fxe4 White has two center pawns but a weaker king. Black hits back with ...e5 at once.
Black keeps the center closed and pins the c3 knight with ...Bb4. White answers with a3 and Bd3.

courses.repertoire: Six main lines, each drilled as White and as Black: the Advance, Exchange, Winawer, Tarrasch, Steinitz and Rubinstein.
courses.summary: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5: Black builds a solid center and hits back with ...c5.

why.text:
As White, you choose the game: the Advance (3.e5) gains space, the Exchange (3.exd5) keeps it simple, and 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2 keep the tension in the center.

As Black, the French gives you a solid position and the same counterattack against almost every White setup: hit White's center from the side with ...c5. Against 3.Nc3 you choose between the sharp Winawer, 3...Nf6 (the Steinitz after 4.e5; 4.Bg5 is under Advanced) and the solid Rubinstein.

rows: Your choice as White; 22% as Black
Black hits d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Against 6.a3, Black locks the queenside with 6...c4 and later breaks with ...f6; White plays on the kingside.
Your choice as White; 30% as Black
Symmetrical pawns and an open e-file. Black develops with ...Nc6, ...Bg4, ...Bd6 and ...Nge7 and castles short; White plays c3, castles and puts a rook on e1.
19% as White, with 3.Nc3; your choice as Black
After 4.e5 c5 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 Ne7 7.Qg4 Qc7, White takes on g7 and h7 and Black takes the center pawns. Sharp for both sides; after 9...cxd4, 10.cxd4? Qc3+ forks White's king and rook.
Your choice as White; 6% as Black
White supports d4 with c3. After 3...Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7, Black breaks with ...c5 and ...f6; after exf6 Nxf6, Black has the half-open f-file and a strong knight on e4, while White aims at e5.
28% as White, with 3.Nc3; your choice as Black
White builds a big center with 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4. Black hits d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6, then plays ...a6, ...b5 and ...b4 on the queenside, and trades the c8 bishop with ...Ba6.
16% as White, with 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2; your choice as Black
Black takes on e4 with the d-pawn, trades knights with ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6, then frees the game with ...c5. Solid for Black; White keeps a little more space.

why.text:
As Black, 2...e6 holds the center with a pawn and keeps the position solid. The cost is the c8 bishop, shut in behind e6, so Black's plans are about freeing it.

As White, taking on d5 early fixes the pawn structure. You know your plans in advance, and there are few early tactics to calculate.

rows: Play Bg5, e3, Bd3 and Qc2, and castle. Then the minority attack (Rb1, b4, b5), or Nge2, f3 and e4.
Play ...Be7 and castle. Against 5.Bf4, hit the center with ...c5. Against 5.Bg5, play ...h6 and the Tartakower.
The Tartakower: ...Be7, castle, ...h6 and ...b6, then ...Bb7, or ...Be6 after 8.cxd5 and the trades on d5. If White takes on f6, take back with the bishop.
5.e4 gains time on the knight and builds a full center.
Against 5.Bg5, play 5...Nbd7, which sets the Elephant trap. Then ...c6, ...Be7, castle, ...Re8 and ...Nf8.
Take on d5 anyway. With no knight on f6 to pin, the bishop goes to f4.

courses.repertoire: As White: the d3 system, with 5.d3 against 4...Nf6 and 4.d3 against the Berlin, then c3, Re1, Nbd2–f1–g3 and d4 later. As Black: the Berlin Defense, 3...Nf6, taking on e4 after 4.O-O.
courses.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5: the bishop hits the knight that guards e5.

why.text:
As White, the Ruy Lopez follows the opening principles: every move develops a piece or fights for the center, and the bishop on b5 keeps Black busy defending e5. It is one of the most popular openings at every level, from club players to world champions, and its plans teach a great deal about maneuvering. This course plays the d3 system: the same setup and plans as the main lines, with far less to learn by heart.

As Black, the Berlin Defense, 3...Nf6, hits e4 at once and gives a solid game. Vladimir Kramnik made it famous in his 2000 world title match against Garry Kasparov, who could not beat it, and top players have trusted it ever since. Against the common 4.O-O, Black takes the pawn and gets the two bishops, and the plans are few and clear.

rows: c3, castle, Re1, then Nbd2–f1–g3 and h3. Push d4 when the setup is ready. Against ...Na5, the bishop drops back to c2.
4.d4 and take back on d4 with the knight. Trade on c6 to double Black's pawns, then b3, Bb2 and f4.
Take back with the d-pawn. After 7.Nxe5 Be7 and castling, Black has the two bishops and active pieces.
...Be7, trade knights on e5 and castle. Then ...Bf6 hits the rook, and the rooks come off on the e-file.
...Nd6, and take back on c6 with the d-pawn. After the queen trade, the king goes to e8, then ...h5 and ...Rh6. Keep pieces on.

As White: c3, castle, Re1, Nbd2–f1–g3, then d4. If e5 is guarded only by the knight, Bxc6 and Nxe5 win it.
As Black: ...Bc5, castle, ...d6, then ...a6, ...Ba7 and ...Ne7–g6.
Take back with the d-pawn, play ...Bd6 and castle. Against 5.Nxe5, ...Qd4 wins the pawn back.
4...Bb4, castle, and take on c3 to double White's pawns. Against the pin Bg5, ...Qe7 and ...Nd8–e6.
4.c3, castle, then d4 hits the bishop. Re1 and h3 keep the center safe. Against 4...d6?, 5.d4 wins material.

courses.repertoire: As Black: 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5, or the Modern Variation, 2...Nf6. As White: 2.exd5 and 3.Nc3, and 3.d4 against the Modern.
courses.summary: 1.e4 d5: Black challenges e4 at once and takes back on d5 with the queen or the knight.

why.text:
As Black, 1...d5 makes the game a Scandinavian from the first move, whatever White had prepared, and its plans are few and easy to learn. After 2...Qxd5 and 3...Qa5 you get a solid position with no weak pawns, like a Caro-Kann. The Modern Variation, 2...Nf6, takes the pawn back with the knight instead, so your queen is not chased.

As White, you meet the Scandinavian in about 7% of your 1.e4 games. Black's queen comes out early, so you develop with gain of time and keep a pawn on d4 and more space.

rows:
White: Develop with gain of time on the queen and keep a pawn on d4. Put the dark-squared bishop behind the c3 knight, so a knight jump uncovers an attack on the queen. Castle long and open the center while Black's king is still in the middle.
Black: Build a wall of pawns on c6 and e6, with the light-squared bishop developed outside it first. Watch for knight jumps that uncover an attack on your queen, and castle once your pieces are out.

White: Take the center with the d-pawn and develop: the queen's long retreat gives you an extra move. If Black pins your knight, ask the bishop with h3 and keep the two bishops.
Black: Develop solidly with pawns on c6 and e6 and pieces on the dark squares, for a compact position without weaknesses.

White: Develop the king's knight first, so the queen is not chased yet, and castle.
Black: Pin the knight, bring out the queen's knight, castle long and aim every piece at the d-file. Then take the center with the e-pawn.

White: Chase the knight with the c-pawn and build a big pawn center, then develop calmly behind it.
Black: Strike at that center at once with 5...e5: the queens come off, and your active pieces make up for White's space.

White: Trade knights on d5 and develop, but no White knight is left to chase Black's queen.
Black: Take back on d5, and your queen stands safely in the center. Develop fast and gain space with the e-pawn; if White pushes the d-pawn, castle long and aim your pieces at d4.

White: Try to keep the extra pawn by guarding it with the c-pawn.
Black: Hit the pawn at once with the c-pawn. You are a pawn down for a while, but develop fast, then push the e-pawn to open the d-file toward White's king and win the pawn back.

why.text:
As White, the London is a system: you play the same setup against almost every defense, so you learn one set of plans instead of a book of theory. The c3–d4–e3 triangle is hard to break, the f4 bishop stays active outside it, and Black is the one who has to know what to do.

As Black, you need no new opening: the Queen's Gambit Declined pieces after 1...d5, or the King's Indian after 1...Nf6, meet it well. White's setup is solid but slow, so you can develop in peace and play for ...e5 or ...c5.

As White: e3, Nf3, h3 and Be2, then c3 and Qb3 against ...c5 and ...Qb6. As Black: against Be2 and h3, ...c5 and ...Qb6; against Bd3, ...Nc6 and ...e5.

As White, you play the same first moves against 1...d5 and 1...Nf6: d4, Nc3 and Bf4. The knight on c3 makes the system sharper than the ordinary London. It can jump to b5 and hit c7 as early as move 4, so Black has to answer threats from the start.

As Black, 3...e6 with ...Bb4 and ...c5 needs little theory. Stockfish rates Black equal or slightly better in this course's main lines, and ...Bb4 is Black's best-scoring answer at club level to White's two most common fourth moves.

Jump to b5 at once. After 4...Na6 5.e3 c6 the knight goes back to c3; after 4...Bd6, take the bishop.
Play e3 and Bd3. If Black takes on d3, take back with the c-pawn; if the bishop drops back to g6, push h4.
Play e3, Bd3 and Nf3. Offer the bishop trade against ...Bf5, and take on c5 against ...c5.
Play e3. Then Bd3 against ...Bf5, f3, g4 and h4 against ...Bg4, and h4 against ...g6.

furtherStudy.title: The King's Indian Defense: Step by Step (Chess Lesson 85)
Learn the King's Indian Setup | 10-Minute Chess Openings

courses.repertoire: Seven Basic lines for both sides: the Mar del Plata, the Fianchetto, the Four Pawns Attack and the Sämisch.
courses.summary: Black lets White build a big center, castles behind the g7 bishop, then strikes with ...e5 or ...c5. When the center locks, White attacks on the queenside and Black on the kingside.

why.text:
As Black, the King's Indian lets White take the center, then fights back against it, so the game stays unbalanced, with chances for both sides.

As White, the big center gives extra space, and White chooses the system: the Classical, the Fianchetto, the Four Pawns Attack or the Sämisch.

rows:
White: Fianchetto your bishop too, so your king is safe and Black's kingside attack has little to aim at. Then take more of the center with the e-pawn, and push the h-pawn one square to keep Black's pieces off g4.
Black: Strike at the center with the e-pawn, then press on White's d- and e-pawns with the queen and a rook on the e-file.

White: Push the d-pawn forward to gain space and chase Black's knight, then guard the c4 pawn with a knight and the b-pawn.
Black: Play on the queenside instead of in the center. Put a rook on the b-file and push the b-pawn to open lines against White's c4 pawn.

White: Build the widest possible center with four pawns, then close it with the d-pawn. Keep the central pawn majority and aim to push the e-pawn.
Black: Hit the center at once with the c-pawn, before White finishes developing. Then trade off the knight that supports White's e-pawn push, and keep a rook aimed at e4. Black's own chance is the queenside pawn majority.

White: Close the center with the d-pawn and attack on the queenside. Retreat the king's knight so the f-pawn can hold e4, then push the c-pawn to open the c-file.
Black: Send the queen's knight to the kingside and storm there with the f-pawn, then the g-pawn. Both sides race on opposite wings.

White: Skip the knight retreat and attack on the queenside at once with the b- and c-pawns. Aim a knight at e6, the square that Black's f-pawn push leaves weak.
Black: Move the king's knight to the edge to free the f-pawn, then push it. Challenge White's pawn on d5 with the c-pawn.

White: The f-pawn guards e4 and keeps Black's knight off g4. Close the center with the d-pawn, and once the c-file opens, castle short: a king on the queenside would face the open file.
Black: Strike with the e-pawn, then open the c-file with the c-pawn so White can't safely castle long. Then move the king's knight to the edge and push the f-pawn.

White: Keep the tension with a knight move instead of taking the c-pawn. If you take it, Black gets fast development for the pawn while your kingside pieces are still at home.
Black: Hit White's d-pawn at once with the c-pawn, before White's attack begins. Put a knight on the strong central square e5, open the center with the e-pawn, and prepare to push the b-pawn.
table.note: How often: the share of your King's Indian games that reach the line, from the side you play in it, counting all its move orders. Source: Lichess rated rapid and classical games between players averaging 1800 to 2199, October 2026. Rarer lines are in Advanced.

openings.name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
openings.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4
openings.summary: Black pins the c3 knight to fight for e4, and is ready to give the bishop for the knight to double White's c-pawns.

furtherStudy.title: Introduction to the Nimzo-Indian Defense
Main Line of the Nimzo-Indian Defense
Qc2 (Classical) Nimzo-Indian Opening Theory
Complete Nimzo-Indian Repertoire for Black

courses.repertoire: As White: the Classical (4.Qc2) and the Rubinstein (4.e3). As Black: castle against 4.Qc2, 4.e3 and 4.Nf3, and hit d4 with ...c5 against 4.Bg5, 4.Bd2 and 4.a3.
courses.summary: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4: Black pins the knight that supports e4.

why.text:
As Black, the Nimzo-Indian develops two pieces and castles quickly, and the pin on c3 keeps White from building a big center with e4. Black chooses when to give the bishop for the knight, often in return for doubled c-pawns that last all game. The plans repeat from line to line, so there is less to memorize than in most main-line defenses.

As White, you choose the type of game. 4.Qc2 keeps the pawns whole and wins the two bishops after a3. 4.e3 develops quickly with Bd3, Nf3 and castling, and the same setup works against most of Black's replies.

rows:
White: Keep the two bishops and the pawns whole. Pin the king's knight, castle, and slowly prepare a pawn push to e4.
Black: Castle early and put the queen's bishop on the long diagonal to watch e4. Then strike at White's center with the c-pawn and take the open c-file.

White: Trade pawns on d5 at once, pin the king's knight, develop calmly and castle. Then gain space on the queenside.
Black: Keep a solid pawn on d5, put a rook on the open e-file, and bring the queen's knight round to guard the kingside.

White: Take the c-pawn at once, and develop the king's knight before the dark-squared bishop so the pawn on f2 stays safe. Trade pieces until Black is left with a weak isolated pawn.
Black: Win the pawn back with the bishop, develop fast, and free the game with a pawn break in the center.

White: Take the whole center at once with the e-pawn, which the queen protects, and add the f-pawn for more space. The two bishops and the f-file give White the better game.
Black: Give up the bishop for the knight and hold the center with pawns. Castling early walks into a trap.

White: Develop quickly and castle early. The isolated d-pawn is a spearhead: the pieces behind it aim at Black's king, and a knight can jump to e5.
Black: Trade pawns in the center, put the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, and give up the other bishop for the c3 knight to leave White with weak pawns on c3 and d4.

White: Keep the same quick setup and castle. When Black closes the center, push the d-pawn forward for space, then open the kingside with the f-pawn so the bishops come alive.
Black: Give up the bishop to double White's c-pawns, then lock the center with pawns on dark squares so White's bishops have no open lines.

White: Keep the same quick setup and castle. After Black takes on c3, bring the king's knight back toward the center and build a pawn center with the e- and f-pawns.
Black: Put the queen's bishop on the long diagonal to watch e4, trade on c3, and hold the center with pawns on dark squares.

White: Pin the king's knight and close the center with the d-pawn, hoping the bishops will count later.
Black: Give up the dark-squared bishop to double White's c-pawns, chase White's bishop with the h-pawn, and set the center pawns on dark squares. If White plays e3 while the bishop is on g5, the bishop is cut off from the queenside, and ...Qa5 wins material.

White: Avoid doubled pawns and develop quietly.
Black: Trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, castle, and strike in the center with the d-pawn. Then trade off White's dark-squared bishop and attack the isolated d-pawn.

White: Develop the king's knight first and keep several setups open: pinning the knight, a quiet e-pawn move, or the queen to c2.
Black: Castle, hit the center with the c-pawn, and trade pawns so White gets an isolated d-pawn. Then use the plan of the Gligorić System: bishop on the long diagonal, and the other bishop for the c3 knight.

White: Spend a move to win the two bishops, then build a big pawn center to make use of them.
Black: Fix the doubled c-pawns, then attack the weak pawn on c4 with the knight, the bishop and the queen. If White pins the king's knight, ...Qa5 pins the c3 pawn in return.
table.note: How often: the share of your Nimzo-Indian games that reach the line, from the side you play in it, counting all its move orders. As White, it is the share of your games with that fourth move (4.Qc2 or 4.e3). Source: Lichess rated rapid and classical games between players averaging 1800 to 2199, October 2026. Rarer lines are in Advanced.

surveys.name: Replies to 1.e4
surveys.subtitle: The six main openings after 1.e4, each played out to move 4, plus a page for the rarer ones.

rows: The Open Games: both sides fight for the center at once, with quick development and early tactics.
Fights for d4 from the side. Unbalanced, sharp games.
Black prepares ...d5 to challenge e4. Solid, slower games.
Challenges e4 at once. White gains time by chasing Black's queen.
table.note: Share: how often each reply follows 1.e4 in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199.

surveys.summary: Under each board, press ▶︎ Watch the moves to step through the first four moves. The Ruy Lopez, Italian, French, Caro-Kann and Scandinavian link to their courses in this app. Rarer openings, such as the Pirc and the King's Gambit, have a page of their own, linked at the bottom.

surveys.name: Uncommon replies to 1.e4
surveys.subtitle: The Pirc, King's Gambit, Scotch, Petroff, Modern and Alekhine, each played out to move 4.

rows: Black lets White build a big center, then hits it from the side with a fianchettoed bishop and ...e5 or ...c5. Flexible, and often sharp.
White gives a pawn to open the f-file and attack at once. Wild, tactical games where the initiative counts for more than the pawn.
White opens the center straight away. Open, direct play with quick development and few slow maneuvers.
Black counterattacks e4 instead of defending e5. Symmetrical and solid: hard for White to win against.
Like the Pirc, but Black waits with ...Nf6, keeping ...c6 and ...d5 in reserve. Flexible and slow to show its hand.
Black invites White's pawns forward to e5, d4 and c4, then attacks the stretched center. Provocative and unbalanced.
table.note: Share: how often each opening comes up in games that start with 1.e4, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. In the King's Gambit and the Scotch, White chooses the opening; in the others, Black does.

surveys.name: Ruy Lopez
surveys.heading: Ruy Lopez Introduction
surveys.subtitle: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5: the main variations, and the lines the course teaches.
surveys.summary:
White's bishop pins the knight that guards e5, and both sides fight for the center in a long, maneuvering game. Black's main choices are 3...a6, which asks the bishop, and the Berlin Defense, 3...Nf6. The map shows how the variations branch, and the course teaches one repertoire for each side.

The opening is named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who analyzed 3.Bb5 in his chess book of 1561, Libro de la invención liberal y arte del juego del axedrez. He did not invent the move, but he studied it closely, and in English the opening carries his name. Because López was Spanish, it is also called the Spanish Game or the Spanish Opening.

rows: The main line. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O come the Closed Ruy Lopez, the Open Ruy Lopez and the Marshall Attack, each with long theory; this course plays 5.d3 instead. 4.Bxc6 is the Exchange Variation.
Solid but passive: a pawn holds e5 and shuts in the f8 bishop. White takes the center with 4.d4.
Black hits e4 at once. After 4.O-O Nxe4 the queens often come off early, in the Berlin endgame; 4.d3, the Anti-Berlin, keeps them on.
The bishop takes its best diagonal, as in the Italian Game. White gains time against it with c3 and d4.

Rarer defenses: the Bird Variation offers a knight trade on d4, the Cozio Defense develops the knight behind the c6 knight, and the Schliemann Defense is a sharp gambit. 3...Qf6 and 3...Bd6 make up the rest.
table.note: Share: how often each reply follows 3.Bb5 in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199.

surveys.name: Caro-Kann Defense
surveys.heading: Caro-Kann Defense Introduction
surveys.subtitle: 1.e4 c6: the main systems and the nine lines to learn first.
surveys.summary: Black supports ...d5 with the c-pawn and brings the c8 bishop out before ...e6 shuts it in. White's main tries are the Advance (3.e5), the Exchange (3.exd5) and 3.Nc3.

rows: White develops quietly: Nf3, Be2 and castling before anything sharp. Black answers ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6, then brings a knight to f5.
White trades the light-squared bishops at once. Black then plays ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6, and ...Qb6 also hits b2.
Black plays ...c5 before developing the bishop. After c3 and ...cxd4, ...Bg4 pins the knight that guards d4.
White plays c4 and, after the trades on d5, keeps an isolated d-pawn. Black develops with ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and ...Bg4.
4...Bf5 develops the bishop at once and lets White chase it with Ng3. Club players then often play Nf3, Bd3 and a bishop trade instead of the sharp h4.
Black accepts doubled f-pawns for quick development: ...Bd6, castling and ...Bg4.
White develops before playing d4. With the queen on e2 and a bishop on c4, White sets traps on e7 and f7.
After 4.fxe4 White has two center pawns but a weaker king. Black hits back with ...e5 at once.
Black keeps the center closed and pins the c3 knight with ...Bb4. White answers with a3 and Bd3.
table.note: Share: of all Caro-Kann games (after 1.e4 c6), the share that reach the variation (3.e5, 3...cxd5, 4.Nxe4, 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 or 3.f3), by any move order. At its branch: how often the line's own move is chosen where it branches off. Source: Lichess rated rapid and classical games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The Maróczy (Fantasy) is rarer, but it is in Basic by choice. Everything else, such as the Exchange with 4.Bd3 or 4.Nf3, the Tal Variation and the Karpov Variation, is in the Advanced section.

surveys.name: Replies to 1.d4

rows: The closed games: Black stakes a claim with a pawn on d5 at once, so White can no longer play e4 for free.
Black stops e4 with a piece instead of a pawn. The games range from solid (Queen's Indian) to sharp (King's Indian, Grünfeld).
A waiting move that usually transposes: after 2.c4 to the Queen's Gambit Declined (2...d5) or an Indian defense (2...Nf6); after 2.e4 to the French.
Rarer tries that often transpose: ...g6 to a King's Indian, ...c5 to a Benoni, ...c6 to a Slav. 1...f5 is the Dutch (see Uncommon replies). 1...e5, the Englund Gambit, is unsound.
table.note: Share: how often each reply follows 1.d4 in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199.

surveys.subtitle: The Queen's Gambit, the Indian Defenses, and the other main replies.
surveys.summary: 1.d4 usually leads to slower, more strategic games than 1.e4. Against 1...d5, White can skip the Queen's Gambit and play a system such as the London or the Colle: the same setup in almost every game, so they are easy to remember. The London is one of the most popular choices at club level (and works against 1...Nf6 too). The Jobava London, with the knight on c3, is a sharper version of it. The Colle is much rarer and is listed with the uncommon replies. Against 1...Nf6 2.c4, Black plays the King's Indian in about a quarter of club games: Black lets White build a big center, then hits it with ...e5 or ...c5 and attacks on the kingside.

surveys.name: Queen's Gambit
surveys.heading: Queen's Gambit Introduction
surveys.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4: the main ways to decline it or take the pawn.
surveys.summary: White offers the c-pawn to lure Black's d-pawn away from the center. Black declines with 2...e6 or 2...c6, or takes it with 2...dxc4. The map shows how the variations branch, and the courses below teach a full repertoire for each side.

rows: The most played and the most solid. The center often stays closed, so both sides follow long-term plans, such as White's minority attack. 3...c5, the Tarrasch, is the active version: Black takes an isolated d-pawn for active pieces.
Just as solid, and the c8 bishop can still come out. Some lines are sharp, because Black takes on c4 and holds the pawn with ...b5. With ...e6 as well, it becomes the Semi-Slav.
White wins the pawn back, and the game opens up: the pieces come out fast, and each side has a few traps to know.
Not taught here. After 3.cxd5, Black has to take back in the center with the knight or the queen, and White gains time by chasing it. Stockfish: +0.6, slightly better for White.
A gambit, and the sharpest reply. Not taught in the courses: the card below gives the plans for both sides, with the Lasker Trap to avoid as White.
Rarer defenses, not taught here: the Baltic (2...Bf5) brings the bishop out before ...e6, the Austrian (2...c5) hits d4 at once, and the Chigorin (2...Nc6) puts a knight in front of the c-pawn.
table.note: Share: how often each reply follows 2.c4 in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199.

surveys.name: Indian Defenses
surveys.subtitle: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4: the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld, Queen's Indian and Benoni.

rows: Black lets White take the whole center, then hits it with ...e5 and attacks on the kingside. Sharp and double-edged.
The pin on c3 stops e4. Black is often ready to give up the bishop pair to double White's c-pawns.
Black invites a big white center with ...d5, then attacks it with the g7 bishop and ...c5.
Black gives a pawn for lasting pressure on the a- and b-files.
Black opens the e-file and pushes the queenside pawns, while White has more space in the center.
Black controls e4 and d5 from a distance with the queen's bishop on b7. Solid and positional.
Most transpose: 2...e6 with ...d5 becomes a Queen's Gambit Declined (about 10%). 2...e5 is the Budapest Gambit (9.5%, see Uncommon replies to 1.d4); 2...d6 is the Old Indian (4%).
table.note: Share: how often each defense comes up in games that reach 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The King's Indian figure counts every 2...g6 game except the Grünfeld (3.Nc3 d5); the others are measured on the move order shown.

surveys.summary: Black develops the knight first and keeps the choice of setup open. The name is older than it looks: as early as 1884, writers called these openings the “Indian Defence” after Moheschunder Bannerjee, a Bengali player who met the Scottish master John Cochrane in hundreds of games in Calcutta between 1848 and 1860. Savielly Tartakower made the name popular in his 1924 book Die hypermoderne Schachpartie.

surveys.name: Uncommon replies to 1.d4
surveys.subtitle: The Dutch Defense, the Budapest Gambit and White's Colle System, each played out to move 4.

rows: Black claims e4 with the f-pawn, for unbalanced play and kingside chances, at some cost to king safety.
A gambit: Black offers the e-pawn at once and usually wins it back with ...Ng4 and ...Nc6. Best as a surprise.
A quiet White system: d4, e3, Bd3 and Nbd2, then the break e4 opens lines toward Black's king.
table.note: Share: how often each opening comes up in games that start with 1.d4, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The Dutch figure includes games that reach it by 1...e6 and a later ...f5. In the Colle, White chooses the opening; in the others, Black does.

surveys.name: Other first moves
surveys.subtitle: The five first moves you meet most besides 1.e4 and 1.d4, with Black's main replies, each played out to move 4.
surveys.summary: Each opening has one board and a Watch button for each of Black's main replies, played out to move 4 along the moves club players choose most often on Lichess. Under each board, White's plan and Black's plan are summed up in a few lines. No course is planned for these openings yet.

rows: White controls d5 from the side and often fianchettoes with g3 and Bg2. Positional games; after 1...e5 it is a Sicilian with colors reversed.
The most flexible first move: White develops, stops ...e5 and chooses a setup later. It usually turns into a 1.d4 opening, the English or the Réti.
White grabs e5 with the f-pawn: a Dutch Defense with colors reversed. Kingside attacking chances, at some cost to king safety.
White fianchettoes the queen's bishop toward e5 and plays against Black's center from the side. Offbeat, maneuvering games.
White fianchettoes the king's bishop and decides on the center later, often reaching a King's Indian Attack or an English. Slow and flexible.
table.note: Share: how often each first move starts a game, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. For comparison, 1.e4 starts 62% of these games and 1.d4 26%.
